items.title: One More Nine: Kafka Availability During Rolling Restarts
items.summary: AvailabilityWritten by Lukas Majercak, with thanks to Nick Garvey for his help with the investigation. AI disclosure: all of the investigation was done before agents got good and AI was used to refine the wording. Motivation Over the past year, we moved Kafka from EC2 to Kubernetes using Strimzi, migrated its metadata layer from ZooKeeper to KRaft, and upgraded through several releases, from 3.6.X to 4.X.X. We tested these changes carefully, but some failure modes only emerged over time and under particular conditions. Before Kubernetes, we rarely restarted brokers or ZooKeeper nodes outside planned maintenance. Now that we run Kafka on Kubernetes, our platform requires weekly node rotation, and pods can also be evicted during scale-down or under node resource pressure. Restarts are now therefore more frequent, with some occurring outside our maintenance schedule. The first signs of trouble appeared in our support Slack channel. Users reported connectivity errors and growing consumer lag during cluster rolls. We initially attributed these symptoms to older clients or inadequate retry settings and our response often amounted to: “The cluster is restarting; it should finish in about an hour.” That explanation started to fall apart as reports accumulated. We needed rolling restarts to be routine for node rotation, vertical scaling, configuration changes, and upgrades. Over time, we found that the interruptions were not confined to poorly configured clients, but some partitions experienced genuine brief server-side availability drops during rolls. These interruptions had two costs:  User Impact Write interruptions can increase latency, fill producer buffers, and cause delivery deadlines to expire. Applications that discard failed sends, or lose unacknowledged buffered records during a crash, can lose data. Read interruptions increase processing latency and consumer lag. If consumers crash, restart, or stop polling long enough to leave their groups, the resulting rebalances can extend the disruption. Operational Overhead Availability issues draw on-call engineers into investigations, sometimes escalating into incidents and follow-up reviews. These disruptions also erode our confidence in performing routine maintenance.  Background Kafka divides topics into partitions, each of which can have multiple replicas. One replica acts as leader, and followers fetch records from it. Most of our topics use three replicas and min.insync.replicas=2, with producers configured for acks=all. Writes can therefore continue after one replica fails, provided the remaining two stay in the in-sync replica set (ISR) and the leader is available. A partition with only a single in-sync replica is considered “Under-Min-ISR”. Two communication paths matter to this investigation:  Broker <-> Broker Follower brokers send fetch requests to the leader. Leaders track follower replication progress. A follower that stops fetching, or fails to catch up within replica.lag.time.max.ms, can be removed from the ISR. Broker <-> KRaft Controller Brokers send heartbeats to the active KRaft controller. If the broker fails to renew its heartbeat lease within broker.session.timeout.ms, the controller can fence it and remove it from partition ISRs.  ZooKeeper vs KRaft The migration to KRaft also changed how brokers receive leadership updates. In ZooKeeper mode, controllers communicated partition leadership changes to brokers through LeaderAndIsr RPCs. In KRaft, brokers learn these changes by consuming the metadata log. In KRaft, successful heartbeats to the controller do not prove that other brokers or clients can reach the broker’s advertised address. Investigating ISR Drops Misconfigured Topics Some topics were configured with a replication factor of two, or used three replicas with min.insync.replicas=3. A single replica going offline therefore brings the partition below min.insync.replicas. We changed topics that were unintentionally configured this way and added validation to our topic-provisioning component. Segment Recovery This one is a doozy. It gave us our first concrete evidence of a server-side problem and helped explain some incidents, but it could not explain all the failures. When investigating Under-Min-ISR partitions, we found this broker log: Producer state recovery took 1ms for snapshot load and 24789ms for segment recovery from offset ...  Almost 25 seconds? That can’t be good. Searching other broker logs turned up recoveries lasting as long as three minutes! Confusingly, not every long segment recovery resulted in Under-Min-ISR, but some Under-Min-ISR incidents correlated perfectly with long segment recoveries. Producer-state recovery is a normal part of Kafka’s operation, and a long recovery does not necessarily affect availability. The problem arises when recovery overlaps with a partition state transition. We found two operations contending for the same partition lock:  Truncating a partition’s log Partition.truncateTo -> … -> Unified
